paragraphs.ncert_ref: Classification of Elements and Periodicity: the modern periodic law
paragraphs.meaning: Mendeleev ordered elements by atomic mass and had to swap pairs such as tellurium and iodine, whose chemistry contradicted their masses. Ordering by atomic number fixed those inversions, and the modern periodic law states that properties are a periodic function of atomic number. The long form then follows the subshell being filled, giving blocks of 2, 6, 10 and 14 columns, and periods of 2, 8, 8, 18, 18 and 32 elements.

words.meaning: Properties are a periodic function of atomic number, not atomic mass.
words.breakdown: Repeating valence configurations produce repeating chemical behaviour.
words.trap: Mendeleev's mass ordering put argon before potassium by mass but not by chemistry. Atomic number, not mass, is the ordering principle.

words.meaning: A horizontal row whose atoms share the outermost shell number.
words.breakdown: Period 3 has eight elements, from sodium to argon, filling 3s and 3p.
words.trap: The period number is the highest principal quantum number in use, not a count of electrons.

words.meaning: A vertical column whose members share valence configuration.
words.breakdown: Group 1 is the alkali metals, group 17 the halogens, group 18 the noble gases.
words.trap: Same group does not mean identical. Valence electron count repeats; size and reactivity change steadily down the column.

paragraphs.hook: The periodic table is a picture of electron configurations, not a list of names.
paragraphs.exam_note: Questions ask for the block, group or period from a configuration. Highest n gives the period; the subshell of the last electron gives the block.
paragraphs.trap: Helium sits in group 18 but its configuration is 1s², so it belongs to the s block, not the p block.

recall.q: The modern periodic law arranges elements by
recall.why: Atomic number ordering removed the mass-based inversions, such as tellurium and iodine.

recall.q: An element with configuration 3s² 3p⁵ belongs to
recall.why: Seven valence electrons put it in group 17, and the last electron enters a p orbital.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Classification of Elements and Periodicity: atomic and ionic radii
paragraphs.meaning: Across period 3 the radius falls from 186 pm at sodium to 99 pm at chlorine, because ten more protons pull the same shell inward, with the added electrons shielding poorly. Down a group the radius rises as each new shell starts further out. Ions behave the same way, so Na+ is 102 pm against 186 pm for the atom, and the isoelectronic series runs Mg2+ at 72 pm, Na+ at 102 pm, F- at 133 pm and O2- at 140 pm.

words.meaning: A size measure taken from the distance between nuclei in a bonded or touching pair.
words.breakdown: Covalent, metallic and van der Waals radii use different contacts and give different numbers.
words.trap: There is no single atomic radius. Mixing definitions from different columns creates false trends.

words.meaning: The net positive charge an outer electron feels after inner electrons screen the nucleus.
words.breakdown: It rises across a period, which is why the radius shrinks from sodium to chlorine.
words.trap: Effective nuclear charge is not the total nuclear charge. The inner electrons cancel part of it.

words.meaning: Species with the same number of electrons.
words.breakdown: Among isoelectronic ions, the largest nuclear charge gives the smallest radius.
words.trap: Isoelectronic species do not share a radius. Mg2+ and O2- both have ten electrons and differ by more than 60 pm.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M30 118h260M30 118V30'/><path class='d-accent' d='M36 44c60 0 90 26 120 40 40 18 90 24 128 26'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='64' cy='52' r='4'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='238' cy='88' r='4'/><text class='d-label' x='40' y='40'>Na, 186 pm</text><text class='d-label' x='176' y='116'>Cl, 99 pm</text><text class='d-label' x='30' y='140'>radius across period 3</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A falling curve from sodium at 186 picometres to chlorine at 99 picometres across period 3.
paragraphs.hook: Adding electrons usually makes an atom bigger. Losing them always makes it smaller.
paragraphs.exam_note: Ranking questions are common. Compare cations and anions by nuclear charge once you know they are isoelectronic.
paragraphs.trap: A noble gas radius from van der Waals data looks larger than the halogen before it. That is a different measurement, not a broken trend.

recall.q: Which is larger, Na or Na+?
recall.why: Removing an electron leaves the same nuclear charge holding fewer electrons, and removes a whole shell, so the ion is smaller.

recall.q: Among Mg2+, Na+, F- and O2-, the smallest is
recall.why: All four have ten electrons, and magnesium has the largest nuclear charge, so it pulls them in tightest.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Classification of Elements and Periodicity: ionisation enthalpy
paragraphs.meaning: First ionisation enthalpy climbs across period 2 from 520 kJ/mol at lithium to 1681 kJ/mol at fluorine, with two dips that matter more than the trend. Beryllium at 899 exceeds boron at 801 because its 2s subshell is full, and nitrogen at 1402 exceeds oxygen at 1314 because its 2p subshell is half full. Down a group the value falls as the outer electron sits further from the nucleus.

words.meaning: The energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion.
words.breakdown: The first value removes the outermost electron; the second is always larger.
words.trap: The sample must be gaseous. Values from liquids or solids include other energy changes and are not ionisation enthalpies.

words.meaning: The extra stability of an exactly half-filled subshell.
words.breakdown: Nitrogen has three unpaired 2p electrons, so its first ionisation enthalpy exceeds oxygen's.
words.trap: This stability explains exceptions; it does not reverse the general trend across a period.

words.meaning: The enthalpy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron.
words.breakdown: Usually negative: chlorine releases about 349 kJ/mol, fluorine about 328.
words.trap: Fluorine is more electronegative yet releases less energy than chlorine, because a small atom suffers more repulsion when an extra electron arrives.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M30 118h260M30 118V30'/><path class='d-accent' d='M36 108c40-8 60-24 80-28 30-6 40 10 70-6 30-16 50-30 90-44'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='116' cy='80' r='4'/><text class='d-label' x='108' y='66'>dip at B</text><text class='d-label' x='166' y='92'>dip at O</text><text class='d-label' x='30' y='140'>first ionisation enthalpy across period 2</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: An ionisation enthalpy curve rising across period 2 with small dips at boron and oxygen.
paragraphs.hook: The trend is a staircase with two steps backwards, and those steps are the exam question.
paragraphs.exam_note: The standard exceptions are Be above B, and N above O. The reasons are a filled 2s subshell and a half-filled 2p subshell.
paragraphs.trap: Second ionisation enthalpy always exceeds the first for the same element, because the remaining electrons are held more tightly.

recall.q: Nitrogen's first ionisation enthalpy exceeds oxygen's because nitrogen has
recall.why: The half-filled arrangement is relatively stable, so removing one electron costs more than it does in oxygen.

recall.q: Ionisation enthalpy falls down a group because
options: The outer electron is further out and better shielded
recall.why: Each period adds a shell, so the outer electron is easier to remove.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Classification of Elements and Periodicity: electronegativity and anomalies
paragraphs.meaning: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom in a bond attracts the shared pair. On the Pauling scale fluorine is 4.0, oxygen 3.44 and chlorine 3.16, and the value falls down a group as size grows. Some apparent breaks come from the measurement rather than the chemistry: noble gases are reported by van der Waals contact, which is larger than a covalent radius, so argon looks bigger than chlorine without contradicting the trend.

words.meaning: The tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract a shared electron pair.
words.breakdown: Pauling values: F 4.0, O 3.44, N 3.04, Cl 3.16.
words.trap: It has no units and no meaning for a free atom. It exists only inside a bond.

words.meaning: The steady size decrease across the lanthanoids, caused by poor shielding by f electrons.
words.breakdown: It leaves zirconium and hafnium almost the same size.
words.trap: The contraction is small per element but accumulates, which is why it separates elements that should be much larger.

words.meaning: A radius that looks out of trend because a different definition was used.
words.breakdown: Noble gas radii come from van der Waals contacts, not covalent bonds.
words.trap: These values do not disprove the periodic trend. Comparing a van der Waals radius with a covalent one is comparing different quantities.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M24 116h272M24 116V30'/><path class='d-accent' d='M40 110c30-4 50-20 70-40 20-22 36-40 60-52'/><text class='d-label' x='36' y='140'>across a period: increases</text><text class='d-label' x='212' y='44'>F is the highest</text><path class='d-guide' d='M170 40v70'/><text class='d-label' x='176' y='92'>down a group: decreases</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A curve rising across a period to fluorine as the most electronegative element.
paragraphs.hook: The noble gases look huge on a radius chart only because their radius is measured differently.
paragraphs.exam_note: Electronegativity is paired with bond polarity and oxidation state. A larger difference means a more polar bond, not necessarily a stronger one.
paragraphs.trap: Electronegativity and electron gain enthalpy both describe attraction for electrons, but one is inside a bond and the other is for an isolated gaseous atom.

recall.why: Fluorine is 4.0 on the Pauling scale, the highest value, because of its small size and high nuclear charge.

recall.q: Chlorine releases more energy than fluorine on gaining an electron because
options: Fluorine is very small, so the added electron feels strong repulsion
recall.why: Fluorine's small 2p shell packs the incoming electron tightly, and the repulsion reduces the energy released.
